entry.text: In 2014 Singapore's National Library Board (NLB) confirmed it would pulp three children's titles, including And Tango Makes Three, deemed to be against its pro-family stance following complaints by a parent and its own internal review. In 2006 the book was moved from the children's section of two Rolling Hills' Consolidated Library branches, in Savannah and St. Joseph in northwest Missouri, after parents complained.

sources.title: Singapore national library to destroy LGBT-themed children's books (TheJournal.ie, AFP, 11 Jul 2014)
sources.quote: Singapore national library to destroy LGBT-themed children's books Library says three books are contrary to its “pro-family” stance. 11.57am, 11 Jul 2014

sources.title: TheJournal.ie (AFP), same article
sources.quote: The National Library Board (NLB) late yesterday confirmed it would “pulp” three children’s titles deemed to be against its “pro-family” stance following complaints by a parent and its own internal review.

sources.title: TheJournal.ie (AFP), same article
sources.quote: The three books to be destroyed include “And Tango Makes Three” – a true story about two male penguins in a New York zoo which raised a baby penguin – and “The White Swan Express”

sources.title: Penguin book moved from children's section (AP via NBC News, 4 Mar 2006)
sources.quote: March 4, 2006, 10:50 PM EST / Source : The Associated Press A children’s book about two male penguins that raise a baby penguin has been moved to the nonfiction section of two public library branches after parents complained it had homosexual undertones.

sources.title: AP via NBC News, same article
sources.quote: The book, written by Peter Parnell and Justin Richardson, was moved from the children’s section at two Rolling Hills’ Consolidated Library’s branches in Savannah and St. Joseph in northwest Missouri.

entry.note: Venice June 2015 row: sources fetched (Wikipedia Brugnaro, The Local, CBS, RT) do not name this title among the 49 books; not used. Singapore: AFP says destroy/pulp; later reporting (Straits Times, cited by Wikipedia) says two titles moved to adult section instead - not fetched.

entry.text: In 1927 the North Dakota State Library decided not to stock Elmer Gantry. In Boston, sales of the novel could be prosecuted under a law prohibiting indecent and obscene books.

sources.title: Banning Elmer Gantry (Dakota Datebook, Prairie Public, 4 Jun 2022)
sources.quote: On this date in 1927, North Dakotans joined in censoring Elmer Gantry when the North Dakota State Library decided not to stock it.

sources.title: Dakota Datebook, same page
sources.quote: banned in some areas around the country, such as Boston, where sales of Elmer Gantry could be prosecuted under a law prohibiting 'indecent and obscene books.'

entry.note: Boston prosecution threat dated 13 April 1927 per NYT headline 'Boston Bans Sale of Elmer Gantry' (cited by Wikipedia, article itself not fetched); Wikipedia: banned in Boston and other cities.

entry.text: In 1984 a parent petitioned against the use of The Color Purple in an Oakland, California classroom, and the Oakland schools ultimately decided not to remove the book from classrooms. In 2013 a parent challenged the book in Brunswick County, North Carolina.

sources.title: Why parents still try to ban 'The Color Purple' in schools (National Geographic, 22 Aug 2023)
sources.quote: The first major attempt to ban the book occurred in 1984, when a parent petitioned against its use in an Oakland, California classroom.

sources.title: National Geographic, same article
sources.quote: Though the Oakland schools ultimately decided not to remove the book from classrooms, the book has consistently been challenged nationwide since its publication

sources.title: National Geographic, same article
sources.quote: “One can eat from a cafeteria or a dumpster…but one would hope those placed in charge of our children would have exercised better oversight,” wrote one parent in a characteristic 2013 challenge in Brunswick County, North Carolina.

entry.note: Oakland 1984 matches our US 1984 'rescinded' row (challenge, book retained). Israel 2012 row is the author declining publication (BDS), not a state or institutional ban; South Africa row is about the film, per its own note.

row_issues.issue: Author's own decision to decline an Israeli edition (BDS), not a ban; Wikipedia says 'declined publication of the book in Israel in 2012'.
Row concerns the film, not the book; no book ban sourced.

entry.text: On 5 October 1988 India banned the novel's importation, after Syed Shahabuddin petitioned the government of Rajiv Gandhi. In November 1988 it was also banned in Bangladesh, Sudan and South Africa, and by December 1988 in Sri Lanka. In March 1989 it was banned in Kenya, Thailand, Tanzania, Indonesia and Singapore, and the last nation to ban it was Venezuela, in June 1989.
